questions.topic: A table scan in a plan and three ways to end it
questions.learningObjective: Identify a sequential scan in a plan
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, an EXPLAIN plan shows Seq Scan on a large table. What does this mean?

options.text: Every row is read from the table
Rows are read in sorted order

questions.explanation: A sequential scan reads every row of the table. It is simple but costly on large tables, and indexes can avoid it for selective queries.

questions.topic: A table scan in a plan and three ways to end it
questions.learningObjective: End a scan with an index
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, which change most directly ends a sequential scan for a selective filter?

options.text: Add an index on the filtered column

questions.explanation: An index on the filtered column lets the planner switch to an index scan when the filter is selective. The other options do not reduce rows read.

questions.topic: A table scan in a plan and three ways to end it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, how can table partitioning end a full scan?

answer.exemplar: Partition pruning skips partitions that cannot contain matching rows, so only relevant partitions are scanned.

questions.explanation: Partitioning splits a large table into smaller physical tables. The planner prunes partitions whose constraints exclude the query's filter range.

questions.topic: A table scan in a plan and three ways to end it
questions.learningObjective: End a scan by rewriting query
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, a query wraps a column in a function, causing a scan. What fix avoids the scan?

options.text: Remove the function and change data
Create a functional index on the expression

questions.explanation: A functional index matches the expression in the query, restoring index usage. Rewriting may be impractical when the expression is required.

questions.topic: A table scan in a plan and three ways to end it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, when is a sequential scan the better choice?

options.text: When the query returns most rows

questions.explanation: When a query returns a large fraction of rows, sequential scan avoids random index lookups and is cheaper. Small tables also scan cheaply.

questions.topic: A cursor and an offset after a row above the page is deleted
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, page two uses OFFSET 20 LIMIT 20. A row on page one is deleted before page two loads. What happens?

options.text: Page two repeats a row from page one
Page two skips the first row of its intended set

questions.explanation: Deleting a row above the offset shifts all subsequent rows up, so OFFSET 20 now starts one row later, skipping the intended first row of page two.

questions.topic: A cursor and an offset after a row above the page is deleted
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, with 50 rows and page size 10, page 3 uses OFFSET 20. If 2 rows above it are deleted, what offset should be used to keep the same logical start?
questions.explanation: Each deletion above the cursor reduces the number of rows before it by one, so subtract the deleted count from the offset to keep the same logical start.

questions.topic: A cursor whose row is deleted before the next page is asked for
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, a cursor points to a row that is deleted before the next page request. What must the client do?

answer.exemplar: The client must detect the missing cursor row and restart pagination from a known anchor or the beginning.

questions.explanation: If the cursor row no longer exists, the database cannot resume from it. The client needs a fallback anchor or must restart.

questions.topic: A cursor whose row is deleted before the next page is asked for
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, how does keyset pagination avoid cursor deletion problems?

options.text: It stores the full page in memory
It uses the last seen key value, not row position

questions.explanation: Keyset pagination filters with WHERE key > last_seen, so deletion of the cursor row only means the next query starts after the last valid key. It is more robust than row position.

questions.topic: A cursor whose row is deleted before the next page is asked for
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, when a cursor row is deleted, what is the safest server response?

options.text: Silently skip to a random row
Return an error requiring client restart

questions.explanation: Returning an explicit error lets the client restart pagination cleanly rather than receiving inconsistent or partial data. Silent skipping hides the problem.

questions.topic: Overlapping pages and the duplicates an endless list has to drop
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, an infinite list shows the same row twice after a page boundary. Why?

options.text: The row appears on both adjacent pages

questions.explanation: Overlapping page ranges or a changing sort order can cause the same row to appear on two consecutive pages. Deduplication by id fixes the display.

questions.topic: Overlapping pages and the duplicates an endless list has to drop
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, how should an infinite list drop duplicate rows?

answer.exemplar: Track seen row ids in a set and skip any row whose id has already been displayed.

questions.explanation: Keeping a set of seen ids and skipping duplicates prevents repeated display even when pages overlap. Reset the set when the list is refreshed.

questions.topic: Overlapping pages and the duplicates an endless list has to drop
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, what prevents page overlap in the first place?

options.text: Use exclusive upper bounds on cursor values

questions.explanation: Exclusive bounds like WHERE key > last_seen ensure each row appears in at most one page. Inclusive bounds can include the boundary row twice.

questions.topic: Overlapping pages and the duplicates an endless list has to drop
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, why does a changing sort order cause duplicates across pages?

options.text: Rows move between pages as order changes

questions.explanation: If the sort key changes between requests, a row can shift from one page to another, appearing twice or not at all. Use a stable sort key.

questions.topic: A rejected optimistic update and the newer edit a rollback discards
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, an optimistic update is rejected because the row version changed. What does this mean?

options.text: Another edit happened after the read

questions.explanation: Optimistic concurrency checks a version number; a mismatch means someone else modified the row since it was read. The update is rejected to prevent lost updates.

questions.topic: A rejected optimistic update and the newer edit a rollback discards
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, when an optimistic update is rejected, what should the application do?

answer.exemplar: Reload the latest row, show the conflicting changes, and let the user merge or retry their edit.

questions.explanation: Rejecting silently loses the user's work. Reloading and surfacing the conflict lets the user decide how to merge changes.

questions.topic: A rejected optimistic update and the newer edit a rollback discards
questions.learningObjective: Choose between optimistic and pessimistic locking
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, when is pessimistic locking preferable to optimistic?

options.text: When conflicts are frequent and costly

questions.explanation: Pessimistic locking prevents conflicts by holding locks, which helps when conflicts are frequent. Optimistic is better when conflicts are rare to avoid lock overhead.

questions.topic: A rejected optimistic update and the newer edit a rollback discards
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, a transaction rolls back after a conflict. What happens to a newer edit made within that transaction?

options.text: It is discarded along with the rollback
It is saved to a log

questions.explanation: A rollback undoes all changes in the transaction, including newer edits made after the conflicting one. Nothing from that transaction persists.

questions.topic: A rejected optimistic update and the newer edit a rollback discards
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, an UPDATE with WHERE version = 5 sets version = 6. How many rows update if the stored version is 7?

options.text: Zero rows, because the version mismatch

questions.explanation: The WHERE clause requires version 5, but the stored version is 7, so no rows match and zero rows update. The application detects this as a conflict.

questions.topic: A rejected optimistic update and the newer edit a rollback discards
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, what is a lost update?

answer.exemplar: A lost update occurs when two transactions read the same value and both write, so the second write overwrites the first without incorporating it.

questions.explanation: Lost updates happen when writes are based on stale reads. Optimistic or pessimistic locking prevents them by serializing conflicting writes.

questions.topic: A whole row write that overwrites a field nobody meant to change
questions.learningObjective: Explain lost update from full row write
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, an UPDATE sets all columns from a stale object. What risk arises?

options.text: It overwrites fields changed by others

questions.explanation: A full-row write replaces every column, including fields modified by concurrent users, causing lost updates. Partial updates avoid this.

questions.topic: A whole row write that overwrites a field nobody meant to change
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, how should an edit that changes only the amount field be sent?
questions.explanation: Updating only the changed column preserves concurrent modifications to other fields. Full-row writes risk overwriting them.

questions.topic: A whole row write that overwrites a field nobody meant to change
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, what is the difference between PUT and PATCH for row updates?

answer.exemplar: PUT replaces the entire resource, while PATCH applies a partial set of changes, preserving unspecified fields.

questions.explanation: PUT semantics imply full replacement, so missing fields may be nulled. PATCH applies only the provided changes, protecting concurrent updates.

questions.topic: A whole row write that overwrites a field nobody meant to change
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, an API accepts a full object for updates. What safer design reduces lost updates?

options.text: Accept a partial object with only changed fields

questions.explanation: Partial updates with changed fields only, combined with version checks, prevent concurrent overwrites. Full-object updates need extra safeguards.

questions.topic: A whole row write that overwrites a field nobody meant to change
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, field-level concurrency control differs from row-level how?

options.text: It tracks versions per field, allowing concurrent edits to different fields

questions.explanation: Field-level control lets concurrent edits to different fields succeed, while row-level blocks any concurrent edit. It is more complex to implement.

questions.topic: An offline queue and the retry policy that empties it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, an offline queue retries failed sends immediately in a tight loop. What problem results?

options.text: It floods the server and wastes battery

questions.explanation: Immediate retries in a tight loop hammer the server and drain device battery. Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries out.

questions.topic: An offline queue and the retry policy that empties it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, which retry policy best empties an offline queue under transient failures?
questions.explanation: Exponential backoff with jitter handles transient failures without overwhelming the server. Fixed or rapid retries cause congestion.

questions.topic: An offline queue and the retry policy that empties it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, why set a maximum retry count on an offline queue?

answer.exemplar: A max retry count moves permanently failing messages to a dead-letter queue instead of retrying forever and blocking the queue.

questions.explanation: Without a cap, a single bad message retries indefinitely, blocking later messages. Dead-lettering isolates failures for later inspection.

questions.topic: An offline queue and the retry policy that empties it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, an offline queue processes messages out of order after retries. Why?

options.text: Retried messages are requeued behind newer ones

questions.explanation: When a message fails and is retried later, newer messages may be processed first, reordering delivery. Use ordered queues if order matters.

questions.topic: An offline queue and the retry policy that empties it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, why should queue message processing be idempotent?

options.text: Because messages may be delivered more than once

questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery means duplicates occur, so processing must be safe to repeat. Idempotency prevents double application.

questions.topic: A message delivered three times and the consumer that applies it once
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, a message is delivered three times. What delivery guarantee does this indicate?
questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery ensures the message arrives but may deliver duplicates. Exactly-once would deliver once; at-most-once may lose messages.

questions.topic: A message delivered three times and the consumer that applies it once
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, how does a consumer apply a message only once despite three deliveries?

answer.exemplar: The consumer records processed message ids and skips any message whose id was already processed.

questions.explanation: Tracking processed ids lets the consumer detect and skip duplicates. The check must be atomic with the side effect to avoid races.

questions.topic: A message delivered three times and the consumer that applies it once
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, an idempotency key for a payment message should be?

options.text: A unique value per logical operation

questions.explanation: A stable key per logical operation lets the consumer deduplicate across retries and redeliveries. Random or timestamp keys break deduplication.

questions.topic: A message delivered three times and the consumer that applies it once
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, why is exactly-once delivery difficult to guarantee?

options.text: Network and process failures create ambiguity about completion

questions.explanation: Failures make it ambiguous whether a message was processed, so systems usually settle for at-least-once plus idempotent consumers. True exactly-once requires distributed transactions.

questions.topic: A message delivered three times and the consumer that applies it once
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, a consumer sends an email on each message delivery. How to avoid duplicate emails?

options.text: Record the email sent in the same transaction as processing
Send three emails for three deliveries

questions.explanation: Recording the sent email alongside processing in one transaction makes the side effect idempotent. Sending before processing risks emails for failed processing.

questions.topic: A gap in a sequence and the messages that must wait for it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, a message sequence has a gap at number 5. What must the consumer do?

options.text: Process later messages out of order
Wait for message 5 before processing later ones

questions.explanation: Gaps mean a message is missing or delayed. Processing later messages first can violate ordering invariants, so the consumer should wait or buffer.

questions.topic: A gap in a sequence and the messages that must wait for it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, how should a consumer handle messages arriving out of order?

answer.exemplar: Buffer out-of-order messages and process them once the missing earlier messages arrive, respecting the sequence.

questions.explanation: Buffering preserves ordering while tolerating network reordering. A timeout should eventually release the buffer to avoid deadlock.

questions.topic: A gap in a sequence and the messages that must wait for it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, how does a consumer know a gap is permanent rather than delayed?

options.text: A timeout expires without the missing message

questions.explanation: A timeout provides a deterministic way to decide a message will not arrive. Without it, the consumer waits indefinitely and stalls.

questions.topic: A gap in a sequence and the messages that must wait for it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, what property must sequence numbers have to detect gaps?
questions.explanation: Contiguous integers make gaps detectable by comparing expected and received numbers. Random or timestamp values do not reveal gaps cleanly.

questions.topic: A gap in a sequence and the messages that must wait for it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, a permanent gap blocks the queue. What is the safest resolution?

options.text: Move the blocked tail to a dead-letter queue after timeout

questions.explanation: Dead-lettering the blocked tail after a timeout prevents indefinite stall while preserving messages for investigation. Waiting forever or dropping data is worse.

questions.topic: A device that missed a delete and comes back with an old edit
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, a device that missed a delete submits an edit to the deleted row. What should the server do?
questions.explanation: The server should reject the stale edit because the target no longer exists. Recreating or silently applying corrupts data.

questions.topic: A device that missed a delete and comes back with an old edit
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, how do vector clocks help detect a stale edit?

options.text: They compare version vectors to detect missing updates

questions.explanation: Vector clocks track causal history, so a device missing a delete has an outdated vector and its edit is detected as stale. Timestamps are unreliable due to clock skew.

questions.topic: A device that missed a delete and comes back with an old edit
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, how should a sync system reconcile a stale edit against a delete?

answer.exemplar: Compare the edit against the common ancestor and the delete; if the delete removed the row, reject or surface the conflict to the user.

questions.explanation: Three-way merge uses the common ancestor to determine intent. A delete in the server's history usually wins, but surfacing the conflict avoids silent data loss.

questions.topic: A device that missed a delete and comes back with an old edit
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, why use tombstones instead of physically deleting rows?

options.text: Tombstones let other devices learn about the delete

questions.explanation: A tombstone records that a row was deleted, so syncing devices discover the deletion. Physical deletion leaves devices unaware and prone to resurrecting data.

questions.topic: A device that missed a delete and comes back with an old edit
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, when can a tombstone be safely removed?

options.text: After all devices have synced past it

questions.explanation: Tombstones must survive until every device has learned of the deletion. Removing them early risks devices resurrecting the row.

questions.topic: A device that missed a delete and comes back with an old edit
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, a stale edit conflicts with a delete. Which resolution is usually safest?
questions.explanation: Server-side deletes typically win to prevent data resurrection, with the client notified so the user can reapply if needed. Silent client wins risk corrupt state.

questions.topic: A device that missed a delete and comes back with an old edit
questions.learningObjective: Handle offline edit queue on sync
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, how should an offline queue of edits be validated on reconnect?

answer.exemplar: Validate each queued edit against current server state and reject or transform those that conflict with intervening deletes or updates.

questions.explanation: Replaying queued edits blindly can resurrect deleted rows or overwrite newer changes. Validate each against current state first.

questions.topic: A device that missed a delete and comes back with an old edit
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, an HTTP update with If-Match etag returns 412. What does this mean?

options.text: The resource changed since the etag was read

questions.explanation: 412 Precondition Failed means the resource's current etag differs from the one in If-Match, indicating a concurrent change. The client must refetch and retry.

questions.topic: A device that missed a delete and comes back with an old edit
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, why is last-write-wins dangerous for syncing edits?

options.text: It silently discards concurrent edits without merging

questions.explanation: Last-write-wins picks one edit and discards the other, losing data without warning. It is simple but unsafe for concurrent collaboration.

questions.topic: A table scan in a plan and three ways to end it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, after adding an index, how do you confirm it is used?

options.text: Run EXPLAIN and check for Index Scan

questions.explanation: EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan. An Index Scan or Index Only Scan node confirms index usage; Seq Scan means it was not used.

questions.topic: A cursor and an offset after a row above the page is deleted
questions.learningObjective: Explain why offset pagination is fragile
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, why is offset-based pagination fragile under concurrent deletes?

answer.exemplar: Offsets count rows from the start, so any insert or delete before the cursor shifts the window and causes skipped or duplicated rows.

questions.explanation: Offset pagination assumes a stable row order and count. Concurrent modifications invalidate that assumption, leading to inconsistent pages.

questions.topic: A cursor whose row is deleted before the next page is asked for
questions.learningObjective: Use a stable anchor for cursor
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, to survive cursor row deletion, what should the cursor be based on?

options.text: A stable unique key value, not a row position

questions.explanation: A stable unique key lets the next query resume after that key even if the row is gone. Physical location and page numbers are unstable.

questions.topic: Overlapping pages and the duplicates an endless list has to drop
questions.learningObjective: Use a seen set in client
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, where should duplicate detection for an infinite list primarily happen?

options.misconception: server may not know client state

options.text: On the client using a set of seen ids

questions.explanation: The client knows which rows it has displayed and can deduplicate by id. Server-side dedup is harder because it lacks client state.

questions.topic: A rejected optimistic update and the newer edit a rollback discards
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, after an optimistic update is rejected, how can the user retry without losing their edit?

answer.exemplar: Reload the latest row, reapply the user's change on top of it, and resubmit with the new version number.

questions.explanation: Reapplying the edit on the refreshed row preserves the user's intent while incorporating concurrent changes. Blind resubmission would conflict again.

questions.topic: A whole row write that overwrites a field nobody meant to change
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, a read-modify-write cycle without locking risks what?
questions.explanation: Reading, modifying, and writing without locking lets concurrent writes overwrite each other. Locking or optimistic concurrency prevents this.

questions.topic: An offline queue and the retry policy that empties it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, what is the purpose of a dead-letter queue?

options.text: To hold messages that repeatedly fail processing

questions.explanation: A dead-letter queue isolates messages that exceed the retry limit, preventing them from blocking the main queue. They can be inspected later.

questions.topic: A message delivered three times and the consumer that applies it once
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, a consumer processes a message and updates a database. To apply it once, what must be true?

options.text: The email is sent before the DB update
The message id and DB update are committed together

questions.explanation: Committing the processed message id and the side effect together makes processing atomic and idempotent. Separate steps risk partial application.
questions.hint: Atomic commit of id plus effect.

questions.topic: A gap in a sequence and the messages that must wait for it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, a missing early message blocks processing of later messages. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Head-of-line blocking occurs when an early missing message prevents later messages from being processed, stalling the pipeline. Buffering or skipping can mitigate it.

questions.topic: A device that missed a delete and comes back with an old edit
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, why do CRDTs avoid conflicts without central coordination?

options.text: Their operations commute and merge deterministically

questions.explanation: CRDTs are designed so concurrent operations commute and merge deterministically, avoiding conflicts without a central coordinator. They suit collaborative editing.

questions.topic: A table scan in a plan and three ways to end it
questions.stem: In a financial spreadsheet, when should index and partitioning be combined?

answer.exemplar: Combine them when queries filter on a partition key and a selective column, pruning partitions first then using an index within each.

questions.explanation: Partitioning prunes irrelevant data first; an index then speeds access within the surviving partitions. Using both avoids full scans on large partitioned tables.
